bullets: How to count unit cubes, find the volume of a cuboid, and measure liquids in millilitres and litres
slides.heading: Volume: cubes, cuboids, litres
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we count 6 unit cubes, build a cuboid with volume 4 × 3 × 2 = 24, and learn that 1 L = 1000 mL - and by the end you will be able to explain why a taller container does not always hold more.

bullets: Count unit cubes to find volume: 6 cubes fill the first shape
Find a cuboid volume with length × width × height: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24
Measure liquids in millilitres and litres: 1 L = 1000 mL
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: Two arrangements are both made from exactly 6 unit cubes
One is stacked tall and one is spread wide - do they hold the same amount?
slides.heading: Does the taller container hold more?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: does the tall stack hold more, or do both hold the same? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s4 settles this exactly.

bullets: Volume is how much space a shape takes up: count the unit cubes that fill it
For a cuboid, volume = length × width × height, and liquids are measured in millilitres and litres
slides.heading: Count cubes for solids, measure liquids in mL and L
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: count the cubes that fill a solid, and use millilitres for small liquid amounts and litres for big ones.

bullets: Count the cubes one by one: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
Volume = 6 unit cubes
slides.heading: Volume as unit-cube counting
slides.notes: Narrate the cubes arriving one at a time and joining the shape: count aloud with the class until all 6 unit cubes are in place.

bullets: One layer is 4 × 3 = 12 cubes
Two layers stacked give 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 unit cubes
slides.heading: Cuboid volume = length × width × height
slides.notes: Count one layer first - 4 by 3 is 12 cubes - then show the second layer stacking on top: 12 × 2 = 24, which is length × width × height.

bullets: A small cup holds 500 mL and a big jug holds 1 L
1 L = 1000 mL: millilitres for small amounts, litres for big ones
slides.heading: Liquid volume: millilitres and litres
slides.notes: Watch the two containers fill: 500 mL in the small cup and 1 L in the big jug, and stress the conversion 1 L = 1000 mL.

bullets: The tall stack and the wide row are both made of 6 cubes
Same 6 cubes means the same volume, whatever the shape
slides.heading: Watch out: a taller container holds more
slides.notes: Hold the tall stack up against the wide row: both are the same 6 cubes rearranged, so the volume has not changed.

bullets: One layer: 4 × 3 = 12 cubes, and there are 2 layers
Volume = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 unit cubes
slides.heading: Worked example: volume of a cuboid
slides.notes: Talk through the layer working slowly as in scene s2 and name each step as you write it; say: count one layer, then multiply by the number of layers.

bullets: Count the unit cubes in a shape and write its volume
Find the volume of a cuboid 4 by 3 by 2, and write 1 L in millilitres
slides.heading: Your turn: count, build and convert
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the layer count first, then on the conversion 1 L = 1000 mL.

bullets: On your own: find the volume of a cuboid using length × width × height
Explain in one sentence why a taller container does not always hold more
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the layer working in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about counting cubes in your second.
